title: Phillips curve
examples: How does the government use this curve to manage the economy?
Is the trade-off real in modern economies?
What happens if we stay on the short-run curve too long?

explain.say: Today we explore the Phillips curve relationship. It shows inflation versus unemployment rates. In the short run, there was an apparent trade-off. This meant policymakers could choose one over the other.
In the short run, policymakers faced a trade-off choice. Lowering unemployment often meant accepting higher inflation. Conversely, fighting inflation could raise joblessness.

draw.text: Short Run: Low U -> High Inflation

explain.say: However, in the long run, this trade-off disappears completely. The natural rate of unemployment determines the long-run level. Policymacy cannot sustainably keep unemployment below this rate.
The long-run curve suggests the natural rate of unemployment is fixed. This rate is determined by structural factors, not by government policy alone. Inflation expectations play a key role here.

draw.text: Long Run: Natural Rate is Fixed

explain.say: Consider a period of high inflation and low unemployment. This suggests the economy is operating on the short-run curve. Policymakers might then try to cool demand down.
In the real world, central banks use interest rates to manage this. If inflation is too high, they might raise rates to slow spending. This shifts the economy back towards the long-run average.

faq.q: Does the long-run curve mean inflation is always zero?
faq.a: No, it does not mean inflation is zero. It means that unemployment cannot be kept below the natural rate forever. You might also ask: What is the natural rate? Or, Can inflation still happen long term?
asks: Can inflation still happen long term?

faq.q: If we keep unemployment low, does inflation always rise?
faq.a: In the short run, yes, that is the trade-off shown. But in the long run, the relationship breaks down because of other factors. You could also ask: Is the trade-off always true? Or, What determines the long-run rate?

faq.q: What causes the natural rate of unemployment?
faq.a: It is determined by structural factors like labor market rigidities and demographics. These are not easily changed by monetary policy. You might ask: What are structural factors? Or, Is it permanent?

faq.q: How does the government shift the long-run curve?
faq.a: Governments generally cannot shift the long-run curve through standard fiscal policy. Changes usually require deep structural reforms in the labor market. You could also ask: Can policy change the long run? Or, What causes shifts?
asks: Can policy change the long run?

faq.q: Is the short-run trade-off always visible?
faq.a: It is visible when the economy is experiencing sudden shocks or changes in expectations. However, persistent policy actions might cause the curve to shift. You could also ask: When is the trade-off visible? Or, Does it always work?

facts: The short-run Phillips curve suggests a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
In the long run, the relationship between inflation and unemployment breaks down.
The long-run curve is vertical, indicating a natural rate of unemployment.
This natural rate is determined by structural factors, not just policy.

quiz.say: If a government wants to reduce inflation, which action is most aligned with the long-run understanding of the curve?

options.show: Raise interest rates to cool demand.
options.say: Raise interest rates to cool demand.

quiz.why: Raising interest rates makes borrowing more expensive, which slows down overall spending and thus reduces inflationary pressures, moving toward the long-run equilibrium.

wrong.0: Increasing the money supply generally increases aggregate demand, which would worsen inflation.
wrong.1: Tax cuts often boost investment and spending, putting upward pressure on prices.
wrong.3: This is too extreme and might cause a deep recession, which is not the targeted gradual adjustment.

quiz.say: In the short run, if unemployment is very low, what is the typical expected inflationary outcome?
quiz.why: When unemployment is low, the labor market is tight, allowing wages and prices to rise, leading to higher inflation.

wrong.0: Low unemployment means high demand for goods and services, which typically pushes prices up.
wrong.1: The short-run curve suggests that changes in unemployment do impact inflation when the economy is not at its natural rate.
wrong.2: The curve shows that changes in unemployment are linked to changes in inflation in the short run.

quiz.say: Which statement best describes the long-run Phillips curve?

options.show: It is a flat horizontal line.
options.say: It is a flat horizontal line.

options.show: It shifts based on government spending.
options.say: It shifts based on government spending.

options.show: The curve is vertical at the natural rate.
options.say: The curve is vertical at the natural rate.

quiz.why: The vertical nature means that inflation cannot be permanently controlled by setting unemployment below the natural rate.

wrong.0: A flat line would imply that inflation is always at a fixed level regardless of unemployment.
wrong.1: While policy can cause temporary shifts, the long-run vertical position is determined by structural factors.
wrong.3: A downward slope suggests a persistent trade-off, which the long-run theory rejects.
